editorNote: A new Japanese cartridge adventure joins a September of ambitious computers and expansion promises.
morningLine: Mario takes a running jump; Apple faces another turn in its founder’s career.

lead.headline: Super Mario Bros. arrives on Japan’s Famicom
lead.dek: Nintendo sends Mario across a scrolling Mushroom Kingdom on September 13.
body: Japan’s Famicom has a new adventure this Friday, September 13: Nintendo’s Super Mario Bros. The cartridge puts running and jumping at the center of a journey through the Mushroom Kingdom, giving Mario a landscape of obstacles rather than a single fixed screen. This is the Japanese release; it is not a simultaneous worldwide launch.

The game’s instruction manual describes a rescue quest through an enemy-filled kingdom. Pipes, brickwork and gaps turn forward progress into a matter of timing. Mario and Luigi give the familiar brothers a new setting in which the route itself is part of the challenge.

Power-ups change the terms of that challenge. A Super Mushroom enlarges Mario, a Fire Flower supplies fireballs, and a Starman grants temporary invincibility. Each gives the player another reason to investigate the scenery while keeping an eye on the next jump.

The Japanese cartridge is documented at ¥4,900. For Famicom owners, the immediate story is a new Nintendo game with an unusually expansive sense of movement. Its reception abroad remains another story: this week’s arrival belongs to Japan.

stories.headline: Jobs tells Apple board he intends to start another computer company
body: Steve Jobs told Apple directors on September 12 that he intended to leave and form another computer company. The announcement places a fresh question before a company already associated closely with its cofounder’s public identity.

The directors initially showed support and discussed a possible investment, according to the museum chronology of the episode. They asked Jobs to defer his resignation for a week. As this issue closes, an intention and a board discussion should not be mistaken for a completed formal departure.

The distinction matters to Apple watchers. A proposed new computer enterprise is significant news on its own; its eventual products, staffing and relationship with Apple are not settled by this week’s announcement.

stories.headline: COMPUTE! puts the Amiga under the microscope
body: Tom R. Halfhill’s in-depth Amiga review in September’s COMPUTE! examines a machine that puts graphics and sound near the center of the personal-computing proposition. His sessions took place before the introduction, making this a hands-on evaluation rather than an announcement of a new September unveiling.

The Motorola 68000 works alongside specialized graphics and sound support. A palette of 4,096 colors offers an arresting specification, but that figure must not be read as a promise that every display mode shows every color at once.

Speech adds another dimension. The review discusses synthesized speech and text-to-speech conversion, suggesting a computer that can address its user as well as draw on a monitor. The software and peripherals surrounding such abilities will help determine what they mean at the desk.

stories.headline: Atari ST expansion promises fill the autumn calendar
body: September’s Antic surveys expansion plans around the Atari ST, carrying forward announcements from June’s Consumer Electronics Show. The report describes a system acquiring an ecosystem, but much of the merchandise is still a promise rather than a delivered accessory.

Haba’s announced list includes a 10-megabyte hard disk at $499 and a Hayes-compatible modem at $299. Haba, Batteries Included and Rising Star are also preparing productivity programs, giving prospective owners reasons to look beyond the hardware specification.

Atari projects a 256K 260ST at $399 and a drive-equipped 260STD at $499, with October or November shipment contemplated. Those are future plans, not products this newspaper can certify as sitting on September shop counters.

worldAnchor.headline: Air-launched antisatellite weapon destroys Solwind
worldAnchor.summary: On September 13, an F-15-launched antisatellite weapon struck Solwind in space. NASA’s chronology also records scientists’ concern that the satellite was still returning useful solar observations.

bbsNote.headline: SIG Wars: who owns an online community?
bbsNote.summary: Arlan R. Levitan’s “Telecomputing Today: SIG Wars,” COMPUTE! September 1985, printed page 105, examines competition between CompuServe and Delphi. The column recounts earlier events, not a fresh September disappearance.

posts.text: Research note, not an authentic BBS post: Levitan reports that the Delphi MAUG branch vanished in May after a short run, replaced by an Apple SIG with a new sysop. CompuServe retained the original MAUG sysop and divided its Apple community into Apple II, Macintosh and developer SIGs.

Research note, not a fabricated period message: the column says Delphi’s off-shift 1200-bps rate was half CompuServe’s and even Delphi 2400-bps cost less than CompuServe 1200-bps. It questions service ownership of user-contributed messages and public-domain programs, and contrasts contributor benefits on noncommercial bulletin boards.

curiosity.headline: A promised ST accessory holds 500 megabytes on compact disc
curiosity.summary: September Antic looks beyond floppy disks toward a proposed Atari CD-ROM system.
curiosity.detail: The article’s subheading touts a 500-megabyte CD-ROM. This is an autumn product promise reported from June CES, not proof of delivery. Its striking capacity is the curiosity; do not call it an audio CD player or DVD.
